entry.title: FastChat Source Tour: The Controller-Worker Mesh Behind Chatbot Arena

link.title: FastChat Source Tour: The Controller-Worker Mesh Behind Chatbot Arena

entry.content:
Before Chatbot Arena became the leaderboard everyone cites in model release tweets, there had to be a machine that could host seventy models at once, shuffle anonymous battles to millions of visitors, and record every vote. That machine is FastChat, the lm-sys platform that describes itself as “an open platform for training, serving, and evaluating large language model based chatbots.” Its README claims over ten million served chat requests and more than 1.5 million human votes, and the code in fastchat/serve/ is the part that made those numbers possible. This post is a source tour of that serving stack: not the training scripts and not the leaderboard analytics, but the plumbing that turns a Hugging Face checkpoint into an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

FastChat earns a careful reading for three reasons. First, its conversation template registry in fastchat/conversation.py became a de-facto community standard — dozens of projects imported it (or, to the maintainers’ dismay, copy-pasted it) rather than reinventing per-model prompt formats. Second, its model adapter layer in fastchat/model/model_adapter.py is a compact study in extensibility: more than a hundred small adapter classes map a model path onto the right loader, tokenizer quirks, and default template. Third, its architecture is genuinely distributed: a controller process tracks workers, workers host engines, and FastAPI front doors route to them — a shape you can still recognize in modern stacks, even as dedicated servers like TGI (/tgi/) or vLLM’s own engine server (/vllm-2/) have absorbed much of this workload with continuous batching baked in.

The diagram below is the map we will follow. On the left are the two client surfaces — the Gradio web UI that powers the Arena experience and the OpenAI-compatible REST server that lets you point openai-python at localhost. In the middle sits the controller, a registry with heartbeats and two dispatch policies. On the right, the workers: a shared scaffold class, the default Hugging Face worker, and the vLLM variant, all resting on the conversation template registry and the adapter registry.

The FastChat serving mesh: two FastAPI front doors (Gradio web UI and the OpenAI-compatible API server) ask the controller for worker addresses, then stream directly from model workers, which load weights through the adapter registry and render prompts through the conversation template registry.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Conversation, L48 — the dataclass that turns a message list into a model-specific prompt string via get_prompt, L76; every request in the system funnels through it.
  • get_model_adapter, L158 — the registry lookup that matches a model path to one of 100+ adapter classes.
  • load_model, L201 — the device and quantization dispatch that every local worker calls at startup.
  • BaseModelWorker, L27 — the worker scaffold: controller registration, heartbeats, and the FastAPI stream endpoint.
  • ModelWorker, L38 — the default Hugging Face transformers worker, including embeddings.
  • VLLMWorker, L31 — the high-throughput variant that drives an async vLLM engine instead.
  • generate_stream, L62 — the hand-rolled, token-by-token generation loop used by the default worker.
  • Controller, L64 — the worker registry with lottery and shortest-queue dispatch plus heartbeat-based garbage collection.
  • create_chat_completion, L412 — the /v1/chat/completions handler where external clients enter the mesh.

The Conversation Template Layer

The single most-copied file in the repository defines one dataclass and one enum. SeparatorStyle (conversation.py, L16) enumerates roughly two dozen prompt formats — ADD_COLON_TWO for Vicuna, LLAMA2, LLAMA3, CHATML, RWKV, GEMMA and friends — and Conversation carries everything needed to render a chat: a system_template, role names, message history, sep/sep2 strings, stop_str, and stop_token_ids. The branching get_prompt method then assembles the exact byte sequence each model family expects, including the [INST] ... [/INST] wrapping for Llama 2 and the <|start_header_id|> headers for Llama 3.

Templates are registered into a module-level dict with register_conv_template, L698 and retrieved by name with get_conv_template, L708, which returns a copy — so a request can mutate its conversation state without corrupting the registry. The Vicuna template itself is a study in minimalism (vicuna_v1.1, L773): a system sentence, USER/ASSISTANT roles, a single-space separator, and </s> as the round-terminating second separator. You can reproduce a real client prompt in four lines with verified public APIs:

from fastchat.conversation import get_conv_template

conv = get_conv_template("vicuna_v1.1")
conv.append_message(conv.roles[0], "Hello!")
conv.append_message(conv.roles[1], None)
print(conv.get_prompt())
# A chat between a curious user and an artificial intelligence assistant.
# The assistant gives helpful, detailed, and polite answers to the user's questions.
# USER: Hello! ASSISTANT

This layer is also the contract between the API server and the workers. The REST server does not know how Vicuna formats prompts; it asks the worker for its template over HTTP (get_conv, L387), re-materializes a fresh Conversation from the serialized fields inside get_gen_params, L266, appends the OpenAI-style messages, and calls get_prompt(). Template knowledge stays in exactly one place.

The Adapter Registry: One Path In, Any Model Out

When a worker starts it calls load_model, L201, which first resolves an adapter through the registry. The base class BaseModelAdapter, L97 matches everything and simply loads via transformers’ AutoModelForCausalLM; subclasses override match() on path substrings and override loading or the default template. Registration is a decorator — register_model_adapter, L152 appends an instance to a module-level list — and lookup in get_model_adapter tries the model directory’s basename first, then the full path, then raises. VicunaAdapter, L702 is the canonical example: match vicuna, load a Llama-family model, and default to the vicuna_v1.1 template.

load_model then handles the environment matrix: CPU (optionally with Intel AMX/AVX-512 bf16 via IPEX), CUDA with multi-GPU device_map="auto" sharding through accelerate (/accelerate/), Apple MPS with a non-in-place attention patch for older transformers versions, Ascend NPU, and XPU. Quantization is pluggable the same way — 8-bit weight compression through load_compress_model, L109, AWQ checkpoints through load_awq_quantized, L24, and GPTQ through its sibling module. Two more registry helpers close the loop: get_conversation_template, L398 picks the right template for a path, and get_generate_stream_function, L404 swaps in family-specific stream implementations for ChatGLM, Falcon, CodeT5p, ExLlama and others. The default worker in /transformers/ (/transformers/) terms is therefore a thin shell around two lookups plus the generation loop.

From Install to Your First Model

The documented install is one line, with extras for workers and the web UI:

pip3 install "fschat[model_worker,webui]"

Three terminals give you the documented minimal serving stack. Terminal one starts the coordinator (its defaults are localhost:21001 with shortest_queue dispatch, per create_controller, L353):

python3 -m fastchat.serve.controller

Terminal two loads the model and self-registers; wait until you see “Uvicorn running on …”:

python3 -m fastchat.serve.model_worker --model-path lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.5

Terminal three smoke-tests the whole chain without a browser, exactly as the README prescribes:

python3 -m fastchat.serve.test_message --model-name vicuna-7b-v1.5

test_message asks the controller for the worker address, posts to /worker_generate_stream, and prints the reply — if this works, the mesh is healthy. To expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, run the documented API server:

python3 -m fastchat.serve.openai_api_server --host localhost --port 8000

then call it with the standard SDK shape:

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "vicuna-7b-v1.5", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]}'

The documented throughput upgrade is a one-command swap: replace model_worker with python3 -m fastchat.serve.vllm_worker --model-path lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.5 and leave the controller and API server untouched — the vLLM worker satisfies the same worker HTTP contract, so the front doors cannot tell the difference. That drop-in design is FastChat’s best idea, and it is why the Arena could mix local weights, quantized engines, and pure API models behind one interface.

Inside the Request Path

Follow one /v1/chat/completions call. FastAPI validates the body into ChatCompletionRequest, L58 and checks the optional static API key in check_api_key, L109. create_chat_completion, L412 then resolves a worker through get_worker_address, L367, which POSTs to the controller’s own /get_worker_address; the controller’s get_worker_address, L156 either draws a speed-weighted lottery or picks the shortest queue — the queue number arrives via worker heartbeats (receive_heart_beat, L209) and stale workers are reaped by remove_stale_workers_by_expiration, L219.

Back in the API server, get_gen_params builds the prompt from the fetched template and length-checks it against the worker’s tokenizer budget in check_length, L155. Streaming goes through chat_completion_stream_generator, L486, which POSTs to the worker and re-encodes the zero-byte-delimited JSON chunks into proper OpenAI data: delta events. On the worker side the shared endpoint api_generate_stream, L197 acquires a concurrency semaphore, then dispatches into the subclass’s generate_stream_gate, L170 — in the default worker (model_worker’s gate, L104) that yields json.dumps(...).encode() + b"\0" chunks from the generation loop, where prepare_logits_processor, L45 has already installed temperature, repetition, top-p and top-k warpers. The vLLM variant does the same dance but converts parameters into a SamplingParams object and iterates the engine’s async result stream (vllm generate_stream, L67), including client-disconnect aborts. Workers keep the controller updated every 45 seconds from WORKER_HEART_BEAT_INTERVAL in constants.py, which also defines the shared ErrorCode enum used in every error payload.

Arena and MT-Bench: The Eval Side

The serving mesh feeds the research side. In battle mode, the anonymous Arena block pairs two models — local ones via the worker mesh, and API-only ones (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Cohere, and more) through the stream iterators in fastchat/serve/api_provider.py. Every upvote, downvote, and flag lands in the monitor directory, the same code paths that produced the LMSYS-Chat-1M and Arena-33k datasets. On the automated side, the fastchat/llm_judge/ package implements MT-bench: make_judge_pairwise, L137 builds judge objects over question/answer files, and run_judge_single, L135 prompts a strong model to grade answers on a 1-10 scale, with reference answers optionally injected for math and reasoning questions. The Judge class (Judge, L59) is deliberately small — the interesting engineering is in the match bookkeeping around it. Training shares the same foundations: fastchat/train/train.py fine-tunes Vicuna-style models on the conversation templates you just saw, with attention kernel swaps for flash-attention (/flash-attention/) wired in as monkey patches.

Honest Limits

The architecture shows its age in specific, inspectable ways. The repository’s own news section ends in early 2024, and the project now reads as a legacy-but-stable platform: newer stacks — vLLM’s native server, SGLang, TGI, or Triton Inference Server (/triton-server/) — handle continuous batching, token streaming, and multi-GPU scheduling inside one process, while FastChat’s default model_worker path generates tokens one forward pass at a time with a Python loop. For interactive demos that is fine; for production throughput it is not, which is precisely why the vLLM worker exists.

The multi-process design also has real operational cost. A minimal deployment is already three processes plus a front door; each worker is its own FastAPI app with heartbeats, and the controller must be reachable by everything. There is no built-in service discovery beyond HTTP, no dynamic scaling, and authentication is a single static API key. Restarts matter too: the controller is in-memory state, so a crash orphans workers until they re-register.

Template maintenance is a second chronic cost. Keeping two dozen separator styles and a hundred-plus hand-written templates in sync with the hubs’ own chat_template files is unwinnable over time, and the file’s opening plea — contribute changes back instead of copying — is a scar from years of forks drifting. Quantization and engine coupling is the third: the vLLM worker contains compatibility shims for engine-internal renames (tokenizer groups, SamplingParams fields that later versions removed), so FastChat pins you to a band of vLLM releases rather than tracking its head. Finally, the non-streaming paths (generate_gate, embeddings) simply drain the stream generator to completion, which is honest and simple but wasteful under concurrency — a reminder that FastChat was built to answer “can we serve this model at all?” in 2023, not “at what p99?”.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of lm-sys/FastChat: conversation templates, the model adapter registry, the controller/worker serving mesh, the OpenAI-compatible API server, and vLLM acceleration.

entry.title: Flax Source Tour: Inside Linen, NNX, and the Functional Heart of JAX

link.title: Flax Source Tour: Inside Linen, NNX, and the Functional Heart of JAX

entry.content:
Flax is Google’s neural-network library built directly on top of JAX, and it occupies a peculiar position in the deep-learning ecosystem: it is the closest thing the functional-programming world has to a household framework. Where PyTorch gives you a mutable object whose weights live in place, Flax — at least in its original Linen API — insists that a model is a pure function and that its weights are data you pass in and out explicitly. That single design decision explains almost everything else in the codebase: the FrozenDict containers, the init/apply duality, the TrainState bundle, and eventually the decision to build an entirely second API, NNX, on top of the same substrate.

The library is also a survivor. It powered some of the largest open training efforts in the JAX world — big-scale projects in the MaxText family still follow Flax-style patterns — and yet by 2024 the team had concluded that Linen’s ceremony was a tax on everyday users. The result is flax.nnx, a redesign where modules are ordinary mutable Python objects again, with the functional machinery moved behind explicit split/merge calls. Today the repository carries both APIs side by side, and reading the source means reading two philosophies of state management implemented against one compiler.

This post is a source tour of google/flax on main. We walk the Linen module system (nn.Module, setup versus @nn.compact), the transform system (nn.vmap, nn.scan), the parameter containers, TrainState, and then the NNX graph machinery that makes mutable modules composable with JAX transforms. The goal is that after this tour, neither API feels like magic.

The two halves of Flax: Linen (functional modules plus lifts and state containers on the left) and NNX (mutable module graphs with explicit split/merge on the right), meeting at shared JAX pytree infrastructure.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • nn.Module, L979 is the Linen base class. You declare submodules either imperatively in setup, L1391 or inline inside a method decorated with @nn.compact, L476. The class itself never stores parameters — it is a shape of a computation, not its weights.
  • nn.vmap / nn.scan, L834 and its sibling scan, L1153 are the “lifts”: wrappers that take a module method and re-execute it under JAX’s vmap or scan while automatically threading parameter state in and out.
  • nn.tabulate, L174 is the introspection tool. It traces an apply call and renders the module tree, activation shapes, and per-submodule parameter counts as a text table.
  • FrozenDict, L54 is the immutable parameter container that init returns. Its unfreeze, L159 method hands you a plain mutable dict, which is also how gradients get applied.
  • TrainState, L25 bundles step, params, tx, and apply_fn into one pytree so the entire training state can be jax.jit-compiled and passed around as a value. It is built on PyTreeNode, L194, the frozen-dataclass helper that registers classes as JAX pytrees.
  • nnx.Module, L55 restarts the story: submodules and variables are ordinary attributes you assign in __init__, and the object is mutable in place.
  • split / merge, L2268 is NNX’s escape hatch into functional land — merge, L2395 is its inverse — and nnx.TrainState, L300 wraps the pattern for training loops.
  • Rngs, L343 manages named random-key streams; unlike Linen’s ad-hoc make_rng, an Rngs object is itself a variable that lives on the module.

Two APIs, One Library

The most striking thing about the Flax repository is that it contains two complete module systems. Linen is the mature one: every module is a dataclass-like descriptor and all state flows through explicit function arguments. NNX is the redesign: state lives on the object, and the functional view is something you opt into per transform.

In Linen, a dense layer looks like a factory. Inside @nn.compact, nn.Dense, L214 calls self.param to declare its kernel, and the first time the module runs, that call materializes weights from an initializer and a PRNG key. The key comes from make_rng, L1912, which pops a stream named params out of the scope the caller provided. Nothing is stored: run init and you get a FrozenDict of weights; run apply with those weights and you get outputs.

NNX flips the polarity. nnx.Linear, L313 assigns self.kernel = nnx.Param(...) in __init__, and that Variable, L1098 object — whose Param, L2035 subclass marks it as trainable — stays on the instance. You call the model like a plain Python object. If you have used PyTorch, this feels immediately familiar; the difference is that every NNX transform knows how to extract the variables, do the pure functional thing underneath, and write the results back.

The bridge between the two worlds is the graph machinery. Because NNX modules form a mutable object graph, JAX cannot trace them directly. nnx.split walks the graph and flattens it into a GraphDef (static topology) plus one or more State, L221 mappings (the actual arrays); merge rebuilds a live module from those pieces. Filters let you split only some variable types — nnx.split(model, nnx.Param) for parameters, a different filter for batch statistics — which is how NNX reproduces the collection-based separation Linen did with named collections.

From Install to Your First Model

Flax installs from PyPI with pip install flax. It pulls in JAX automatically; whether you get GPU or TPU acceleration depends on the JAX backend you install alongside it, exactly as with any JAX program. There is no compiled extension to build and no system dependency to hunt down.

Here is a complete NNX model, taken almost verbatim from the docstring of the module class itself:

import jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx

class Model(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, rngs):
        self.linear1 = nnx.Linear(2, 3, rngs=rngs)
        self.linear2 = nnx.Linear(3, 4, rngs=rngs)
    def __call__(self, x):
        x = self.linear1(x)
        x = nnx.relu(x)
        return self.linear2(x)

model = Model(rngs=nnx.Rngs(0))
y = model(jnp.ones((1, 2)))

Every constructor that creates variables takes rngs= — an Rngs object that hands out named key streams. From there you can drop into the functional view whenever you need it:

graphdef, params = nnx.split(model, nnx.Param)
# ... inspect or serialize `params` as a pytree ...
model = nnx.merge(graphdef, params)

And the training-loop idiom is to let nnx.jit (flax/nnx/transforms/compilation.py, L200) handle the split/merge sandwich for you: you write an ordinary function that mutates the model, decorate it with @nnx.jit, and the transform extracts state before the call and applies updates after it. For comparison, the same model in Linen requires an init call to produce a parameter tree and an apply call for every forward pass — apply, L2090 takes the params as its second argument, while init, L2314 creates them from an RNG key. One API treats state as a detail; the other makes it the interface.

The Functional Core: init, apply, and FrozenDict

Linen’s design is easiest to understand as a discipline imposed on JAX. JAX’s jit and grad want pure functions over pytrees, so Flax makes the model a pure function and the parameters a pytree. The pytree in question is FrozenDict, a hash-frozen, immutable mapping. Immutability is not aesthetic: it guarantees that a traced computation cannot silently mutate the weights it was compiled against, and it makes parameter trees safe to share across threads and cache across jit calls.

To update parameters you call unfreeze, apply your gradient, and re-wrap — or, more commonly, you let TrainState do it. Its apply_gradients, L81 method takes gradients and returns a new TrainState with updated params and an incremented step counter, and its create, L125 classmethod wires up the optimizer from optax. Because the whole object is a pytree (courtesy of PyTreeNode), one jax.jit covers the step function. This pattern spread far beyond Flax — plenty of JAX codebases that never adopted Linen still have a TrainState-shaped object at their center.

There is a subtlety worth knowing: parameters are not the only state. self.param declares read-only variables in the params collection, while the more general variable, L1720 method can declare mutable collections — batch_stats for normalization running means, cache for autoregressive decoding, anything you name. apply accepts mutable=[...] to say which collections may change, and returns them alongside the output. NNX generalizes this: every variable carries its type, and filters select by type, so the collection idea became a class hierarchy.

Lifts: vmap, scan, and Friends

The transforms are where Flax earns its complexity budget. nn.vmap maps a module method over a batch axis, but unlike raw jax.vmap it also maps the parameters: each logical “member” of the mapped module gets its own slice of the parameter tree, sliced automatically along the axes you nominate. nn.scan does the same for a loop over time, threading carry state through iterations and stacking the per-step outputs.

Implementing this on immutable state is genuinely intricate — the lift has to track which variables are mapped, which are carried, and which are broadcast, then reassemble the state after the call — which is why the file runs well over a thousand lines and sits on flax.core.lift, the lower-level lifting machinery. On top of it, scan_with_axes, L416 and vmap_with_axes, L472 in the partitioning module add support for AxisMetadata, so that sharding annotations survive the lift — the detail that made large-scale MaxText-style training practical in Flax.

NNX re-derived all of this for the object world. nnx.vmap, L398 and nnx.scan, L1499 split the module, perform the lifted computation on pytrees, and merge the mutated state back into the live objects afterward. The supporting helpers split_inputs, L43 and merge_inputs, L172 convert module arguments into jax-compatible data so that arbitrary transforms can be applied without special-casing every call site. The user-facing result is nicer — you decorate a method, not a class — but the source shows the same conceptual machinery underneath, just relocated from the caller’s hands into the library’s.

TrainState and the Training Loop

A canonical Linen training step is almost boring in its regularity: build a TrainState once with create, then loop grads = grad(loss)(state.params), state = state.apply_gradients(grads=grads), all under one jit. The step counter, optimizer, and parameters travel together, which makes checkpointing trivial — the entire training state is one pytree you can serialize, and libraries in the wider JAX orbit (including the Hugging Face transformers JAX integrations in their day) adopted the shape.

NNX’s nnx.TrainState mirrors the idea, but because the module is mutable, the class is generic over the module type and uses split/merge internally to expose a functional surface. Notably, its source imports the struct helper from flax.training.train_state — the two APIs share their pytree plumbing even where their surfaces diverge. If you are porting a Linen codebase, this is the pattern to lean on: keep the TrainState-shaped loop, swap the module construction and the apply call, and let the graph machinery handle the stateful parts.

One practical wrinkle: in NNX the “which variables are trainable” question is answered by filters at the split site, so the same module can be wrapped differently for training versus evaluation — parameters only, or parameters plus batch statistics. It is flexible, but it moves a decision that Linen encoded in collection names into your call sites.

Honest Limits

The dual-API situation is the elephant. If you read Flax documentation today, you will find NNX presented as the recommended path while enormous amounts of production code — and many published code examples, checkpoints, and university course materials — are Linen. The two APIs are close enough in spirit that translation is mechanical, but not drop-in: collection strings become variable-type filters, setup becomes __init__, and the mutable= argument becomes filter lists. Teams carry both mental models, and the repository carries both test suites and both summary tools (nn.tabulate for Linen, the object-level display machinery for NNX).

The functional ceremony is the second real cost. In Linen, a beginner’s first training loop involves concepts PyTorch never asks for: separate init and apply, immutable dictionaries, named RNG streams, and the mutable= flag. None of it is gratuitous — each piece exists because JAX needs purity — but the on-ramp is objectively steeper, and error messages when you pass the wrong state shape can be opaque. NNX fixes much of the ergonomics at the price of a new set of rules about when state is extracted and re-applied, and transform interactions (scan over a module that jits another module) still require care in either API.

Finally, the docs lag the code in places. The NNX API has moved fast — module, variable, and state internals were reworked repeatedly — so blog posts and Stack Overflow answers often describe stale signatures. Check the source before trusting a snippet: the repository is well-commented, docstrings carry doctests, and as this tour shows, the whole system is small enough to read in an afternoon. If you want the compiler-side context for why all this functional machinery exists, our JAX tour is the natural next stop; for a different take on the same mutable-object problem, Keras shows what a framework looks like when it hides the functional layer entirely.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Google's Flax: Linen modules and transforms, the newer NNX API, FrozenDict state, TrainState patterns, and how a JAX training loop fits together.

entry.title: KerasHub Deep Dive: The Pretrained-Model Hub That Makes Keras 3 Feel Like a Model Zoo

link.title: KerasHub Deep Dive: The Pretrained-Model Hub That Makes Keras 3 Feel Like a Model Zoo

entry.content:
Most deep learning work in 2026 starts from a checkpoint, not from a blank model. You pick an architecture, download pretrained weights, attach a small head or a prompt, and start training. KerasHub is the keras-team’s answer to that workflow: a library of pretrained vision, text, audio and multimodal models built as honest Keras layers first, so they compose with the rest of the Keras 3 ecosystem rather than living beside it. Where the Hugging Face Transformers stack grew from a modeling library into an ecosystem of its own abstractions, KerasHub took the opposite bet: keep the surface area small, make every pretrained model a keras.Model you can fit(), compile(), save() and inspect with the tools you already know.

The library covers a wide menu — BERT, Gemma, Gemma 3, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Whisper, SAM, ResNet, RetinaNet, diffusion models — but the genuinely interesting engineering lives underneath the model menu, in roughly a dozen files under keras_hub/src. There you find a three-base class hierarchy (Backbone, Task, CausalLM), a checkpoint registry that resolves four different handle schemes including Kaggle Models and Hugging Face, tokenizer layers that are themselves Keras layers, and a generation system with per-backend compiled fast paths. This post walks that framework layer by layer, reading real code from the current master branch (checked out at commit 3ba52a2, which lands EmbeddingGemma2).

One structural note before we dive in: this is a library of libraries post. KerasHub depends on Keras 3, and Keras 3 dispatches every keras.ops call to TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch, OpenVINO or NumPy at runtime. That single decision shapes almost every file we will read — most obviously in how generation gets compiled, which we will see in detail below.

The KerasHub skeleton: the public API re-exports two base classes and a preset registry; task models wrap backbones, presets resolve to Kaggle or Hugging Face handles, and tokenizers feed everything.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Task, L22 is the base class for every end-to-end model: it wraps a Backbone plus a Preprocessor and wires automatic preprocessing into fit(), predict() and evaluate().
  • Backbone, L11 is the architecture-only base — hidden states in, hidden states out — with from_preset, LoRA helpers and Hugging Face export.
  • CausalLM, L20 extends Task with a sampler argument on compile() and the famous string-in/string-out generate() method.
  • get_preset_loader, L553 inspects a preset’s config.json and dispatches to a Keras, Transformers or timm loader — this is how hf:// checkpoints load at all.
  • get_file, L133 resolves a preset identifier to a local path across kaggle://, hf://, modelscope://, gs:// and plain directories.
  • SentencePieceTokenizer, L32 and BytePairTokenizer, L217 are the two workhorse tokenizer layers.
  • GemmaCausalLM, L14 shows what a concrete model contributes on top of the bases: a KV-cache forward pass and a compilable generation step.
  • Sampler, L10 is the base class for decoding strategies — greedy, top-k, beam, contrastive, even speculative sampling.

Backbone, Task, CausalLM: The Three-Bases Design

The split between Backbone and Task is the load-bearing idea. A Backbone subclasses keras.Model but is deliberately not tied to any loss: it outputs final hidden states, nothing more. Its constructor builds the layers first — embeddings, transformer stack, final norm — then wires them into a functional keras.Model via keras.Inputs. That functional-model trick matters more than it looks: because all weights are owned by a functional graph, the standard Keras saving, cloning and distribution machinery works without per-model customization. The class even routes around backend quirks in __setattr__ with an explicit torch-backend branch, a small but honest acknowledgment that “write once, run on three backends” has edges.

Task adds the product-facing half. A task owns a backbone and an optional preprocessor, and its preprocess_samples, L64 hook feeds raw strings or images through the preprocessor inside fit() and predict() — set model.preprocessor = None and you drop back to dense tensors. Two other methods deserve attention. First, quantize, L104 overrides Keras quantization to skip preprocessing layers entirely, because tokenizers hold no quantizable weights and are often unbuilt at quantize time, which would otherwise crash. Second, weight bookkeeping is split: load_task_weights, L232 and save_task_weights handle only weights that live outside the backbone (a classification head, for instance), storing them in a separate task.weights.h5 while the backbone’s shard loads independently. summary() is also overridden to print the preprocessor’s tokenizer vocabulary size using a rich-formatted table.

CausalLM then layers generation on top. Its compile, L63 accepts optimizer="auto", loss="auto" defaults — Adam at 2e-5, sparse cross-entropy — plus a sampler argument resolved through a small serialization helper. The heart is generate, L284, which normalizes inputs, preprocesses, distributes tensors, runs a compiled per-batch generation function, and postprocesses back to strings. The compilation itself happens in make_generate_function, L130: on TensorFlow it wraps generate_step in a tf.function with jit_compile; on JAX it goes further, packing sampler variables, trainable and non-trainable variables into an explicit state tuple and running under jax.jit inside a keras.StatelessScope, reassigning only the sampler’s random-seed variables afterwards; on PyTorch it is a simple torch.no_grad() wrapper. Same API, four different execution realities — that is multi-backend in practice, not in marketing.

from_preset: One Registry, Four Handle Schemes

Every base class exposes from_preset(preset, load_weights=True, **kwargs), and the preset machinery in keras_hub/src/utils/preset_utils.py is the most architecturally interesting file in the repo. The registry itself is two module-level dictionaries: BUILTIN_PRESETS, L74 maps short names like "gemma_2b_en" to metadata, and register_presets, L78 fills it from per-model preset tables at import time. Each entry’s crucial field is a kaggle_handle — the short name is just sugar for a Kaggle Models URI.

Resolution happens in get_file, L133. A kaggle://org/model/keras/variant handle goes through kagglehub.model_download, with careful error translation: a 404 becomes a missing-file error while a 403 becomes “if this model is gated, accept its terms on kaggle.com and retry” — the kind of error message you only write after being bitten. An hf://org/model handle calls hf_hub_download; modelscope:// delegates to ModelScope; a bare path is treated as a local directory; and GCS-style URIs ride TensorFlow’s gfile into the local ~/.keras cache.

The loader dispatch is where cross-ecosystem compatibility lives. get_preset_loader reads the preset’s config.json and inspects one key: registered_name means a serialized Keras object (the native format), model_type means a Hugging Face Transformers config, architecture means timm. So TransformersPresetLoader, L50 can construct a KerasHub backbone directly from a HF repo, mapping weights out of the safetensors shards (for background on that format, see the safetensors tour). The Keras loader’s load_task, L705 assembles backbone, preprocessor and task weights, resolving dtype policies so a bfloat16-saved checkpoint casts cleanly to the current default. Saving is symmetric through KerasPresetSaver and a public keras_hub.upload_preset function, which even generates a starter HF model card on first upload. And when you want to leave the ecosystem, export_to_transformers writes HF-compatible output via export_to_safetensors, L402.

Tokenizer Layers That Behave Like Keras Layers

The second quiet idea in KerasHub is that tokenization is a layer, not a function. Tokenizer, L24 subclasses PreprocessingLayer and declares tokenize, detokenize, vocabulary_size and token_to_id — which means a tokenizer can be serialized inside a keras.Model, shipped in a preset, and restored with assets. (If you want a deeper comparison of tokenizer architectures in general, the tokenizers tour covers the fast-Rust design this layer deliberately does not use.)

SentencePieceTokenizer maintains two execution paths behind one API: a TensorFlow Text SentencepieceTokenizer that runs inside the TF graph — essential for saving the tokenizer into a standalone model — and a pure sentencepiece Python path used everywhere else, including JAX and PyTorch. The proto itself is cleverly persisted: set_proto, L167 base64-encodes the model bytes into the config, dodging Keras’s inability to serialize bytestrings, and caches vocabulary metadata eagerly so vocabulary_size() never touches TF at trace time.

BytePairTokenizer reimplements the OpenAI GPT-2 encoder but TF-graph-compatible, including a regex-splitting trick that substitutes a rare character placeholder for unsplittable special tokens — and it ships the Llama3 split pattern as a built-in constant, which is how LlamaTokenizer matches Meta’s reference behavior token-for-token.

From Install to Your First Model

The install is one package plus whichever backend you favor:

pip install keras-hub
# optional but recommended:
pip install kagglehub huggingface_hub sentencepiece

Then a generative model is three lines, exactly as advertised in the class docstrings:

import keras_hub

gemma_lm = keras_hub.models.GemmaCausalLM.from_preset("gemma_2b_en")
gemma_lm.compile(sampler="top_k")
print(gemma_lm.generate("KerasHub is", max_length=64))

from_preset downloads config.json, the tokenizer, and the weights shard from Kaggle, builds a GemmaBackbone, attaches a GemmaCausalLMPreprocessor, and returns a task ready for both generate() and fit(). Fine-tuning on raw strings is a fit() call with a batch size, and parameter-efficient tuning is built in: call enable_lora, L195 with a rank, which freezes the whole backbone and lora-fies only the query/value einsum-dense layers whose names come from default_lora_layer_names, L191. The LoRA factors then save and reload through save_lora_weights/load_lora_weights in a tiny .lora.h5 file, keyed by layer index rather than layer name — names are not unique across a deep stack, and the comment in the code says exactly that.

Gemma and Llama: One Skeleton, Two Personalities

Concrete models then implement the bases. GemmaBackbone builds a tied ReversibleEmbedding, L107 whose output gets multiplied by sqrt(hidden_dim) — the Gemma-specific embedding scaling — then stacks GemmaDecoderBlock, L14 units, each pairing RMSNorm with a CachedGemmaAttention, L17 that supports grouped-query heads, attention logit soft caps, and sliding-window attention on alternating layers. For anyone scaling to multiple accelerators, get_layout_map, L213 returns a keras.distribution.LayoutMap sharding embedding and FFW kernels tensor-parallel while attention outputs go data-parallel — model parallelism as a static layout map, not a rewrite.

The task side is where inference engineering shows. call_with_cache, L174 runs one forward pass against a preallocated key/value cache of shape [batch, layers, 2, max_length, heads, head_dim], updating each layer’s slice at cache_update_index; generate_step, L230 seeds that cache with a full prompt pass, then hands a next() closure to the sampler so decoding strategy and model math stay decoupled. There is even a public score() method for interpretability work, returning per-token logits or losses with an interception hook between layers. Llama follows the same skeleton with its own flavor: LlamaBackbone plus LlamaAttention, L15 grouped-query attention — and if you care about throughput-critical serving rather than in-process generation, dedicated engines like vLLM remain the right tool; KerasHub’s advantage is that the same object you generated with is the one you fine-tuned.

Honest Limits

No source tour is complete without the trade-offs, and KerasHub has real ones.

Preset downloads route through Kaggle. Every built-in short name is a kaggle:// handle underneath, so the first run of from_preset needs network access and, for gated models like Llama, an accepted license on kaggle.com — the 403 path we saw in get_file. Air-gapped environments need a pre-populated cache or a local preset directory, which works but is on you to assemble.

Multi-backend means multi-performance. Four generate paths means four performance profiles. The JAX path re-wraps state into a StatelessScope for jax.jit; the TF path depends on jit_compile surviving Keras version changes; the torch path is the plainest but historically the least optimized. Same code, and benchmarks across backends routinely differ by multiples — pick your backend by measurement, not preference. Server deployments that demand best latency (vLLM, TensorRT-style engines) will beat any of these paths.

The model menu is smaller than Hugging Face’s. The TransformersPresetLoader closes much of the gap — many popular HF checkpoints load directly — but KerasHub’s natively supported architecture list is a few dozen families, not tens of thousands, and weight mapping is one-to-one per architecture: a new HF architecture works only after someone writes its converter.

Keras 3 version coupling. The code checks at runtime whether your Keras supports sharded weight loading, keras.dtype_policies.get existed only after Keras 3.2, and the torch-backend __setattr__ workarounds are pinned to current Keras internals. Upgrading KerasHub usually means upgrading Keras, and occasionally that upgrade is not optional.

None of these are disqualifying — they are the cost of the bet KerasHub makes: one model object that is simultaneously a Keras layer, a Kaggle-downloadable checkpoint, a trainable network on any of three major backends, and an exportable artifact. Read alongside the Keras 3 source and the Transformers library, it is a masterclass in how little framework a model zoo actually needs.
entry.summary: A source tour of KerasHub: Task and Backbone abstractions, the from_preset checkpoint registry, SentencePiece and byte-pair tokenizers, Gemma and Llama implementations, LoRA fine-tuning and true multi-backend inference.

entry.title: TensorRT Model Optimizer: A Source Tour of NVIDIA’s Model Compression Toolkit

link.title: TensorRT Model Optimizer: A Source Tour of NVIDIA’s Model Compression Toolkit

entry.content:
Most inference stacks spend their lives downstream of a model. NVIDIA’s Model Optimizer — ModelOpt for short — lives upstream, where the model itself is made smaller. The repository, NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer on GitHub, is the source behind the nvidia-modelopt PyPI package: a library of compression techniques covering post-training quantization, quantization-aware training, weight and attention sparsity, structured pruning, distillation, and speculative decoding. Its README states the contract plainly: you bring a Hugging Face, PyTorch, or ONNX model; ModelOpt hands back an optimized, quantized checkpoint that downstream engines like vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and TensorRT can execute at reduced precision.

What makes the codebase worth a source tour is its architecture. Almost every technique is expressed as a mode — a self-describing object that knows how to rewrite a model, how to restore it, and how to serialize its own state. That uniformity is why a quantization call and a sparsification call look nearly identical in user code, even though one swaps nn.Linear for a fake-quantized replica and the other replaces dense attention with a masked kernel. It is also why the library can chain techniques — prune, distill, quantize, export — through one shared state manager.

This post walks the main branch as of October 2026. We map the package from its three public facades down through the quantization engine, the low-precision tensor implementations, the sparsity and pruning searchers, and the export layer that turns a quantized model into something an inference server can load. Every symbol we cite links to its actual line in the repository.

Overview: the three public namespaces (mtq, mts, mtp) sit on top of a shared mode framework; the quantization core rewrites layers and fills calibrator statistics; results flow into the Hugging Face export and the model-free ONNX path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • mtq namespace, L26 — the quantization facade imports compress, config, and conversion submodules into one flat namespace, so mtq.quantize(...) is a one-liner.
  • mtq.quantize, L310 — the central PTQ entry point that takes a model, a config dict, and a forward_loop.
  • INT8_DEFAULT_CFG, L1699 — preset configurations are loaded from YAML files shipped in the modelopt_recipes package and exposed as module constants.
  • QuantModuleRegistry, L203 — the registry that maps ordinary nn.Module types to their quantized replicas.
  • _Calibrator, L25 — the base class behind max, entropy, and MSE calibration strategies.
  • mts.sparsify, L32 — the weight-sparsity entry point driving one-shot mask searchers.
  • mtp.prune, L31 — the structured-pruning entry that searches over width and depth choices.
  • export_hf_checkpoint, L1871 — the unified Hugging Face export that writes quantized checkpoints deployable in vLLM and SGLang.
  • quantize, L122 — the model-free ONNX PTQ path, for when you have a graph rather than a training-capable model.

One Facade, Five Modes

The spine of the library is modelopt/torch/opt/mode.py. ModeDescriptor, L56 declares what a technique is called, which configuration schema it accepts, and how it should be applied; a private registry class at L277 keeps every descriptor keyed by name. Each technique module defines its own descriptor — QuantizeModeDescriptor, L84 for quantization, one for sparsity, one for distillation — and registers it with the shared machinery at import time.

The payoff is a uniform lifecycle in modelopt/torch/opt/conversion.py. ModeloptStateManager, L64 tracks which modes are currently active on a model; apply_mode, L343 is the single funnel every facade call goes through; and save, L495 serializes mode state alongside weights so a quantized checkpoint remembers how it was made. When quantization/conversion.py’s convert_to_quantized_model, L63 folds fake quantizers into real packed weights, it does so as one conversion step in this same lifecycle, not as a side door.

Five facades share this spine: mtq (quantization), mts (sparsity), mtp (pruning), modelopt.torch.distill (knowledge distillation, whose convert, L32 attaches a teacher for logit matching), and modelopt.torch.speculative (convert, L30, which bolts draft models onto a target for multi-token decoding). Distillation and speculative decoding are also how the library recovers accuracy after aggressive compression — prune a model, then teach the pruned student to behave like the original.

PTQ: Calibrate, Quantize, Convert

Post-training quantization in ModelOpt is a three-act flow. Act one: mtq.calibrate — calibrate, L73 — runs your data through the model while calibrators watch activation ranges. The calibration hierarchy starts at _Calibrator, L25; MaxCalibrator, L26 tracks a running maximum, while HistogramCalibrator, L35 builds histograms that entropy- and MSE-based clipping strategies search for better saturation points.

Act two is the rewrite. mtq.quantize walks the module tree and consults QuantModuleRegistry, L203, swapping each recognized layer class for a quantized replica that owns two children: a weight quantizer and an input quantizer, both instances of TensorQuantizer, L136. During the quantized forward pass each quantizer delegates to the autograd functions in tensor_quant.py — FakeTensorQuantFunction, L332 for integer formats, ScaledE4M3Function, L417 for FP8 — which simulate rounding without changing dtype. That simulation is what makes quantization-aware training possible: gradients flow through the fake-quant math, so a few finetuning steps can restore accuracy that pure PTQ would lose.

Act three is conversion and selection. For deployment you call the real-quantization conversion to pack weights and scales into deployable form; for hard cases there is auto_quantize, L590, which searches over per-layer format assignments under a memory or throughput budget — the mode behind it, AutoQuantizeModeDescriptor, L208, scores candidates by sensitivity, not exhaustive evaluation. A KV-cache specialist, kv_cache_auto_quant.py, searches per-layer KV formats automatically.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one line from the README:

pip install -U nvidia-modelopt[all]

The [all] extra pulls in the framework plugins (Hugging Face Transformers, diffusers, and friends) that ModelOpt discovers lazily at import. The canonical quantization snippet below is taken verbatim from the module docstring of modelopt/torch/quantization/config.py (lines 132–135), which is the same pattern every example in the repository uses:

import modelopt.torch.quantization as mtq

def forward_loop(model):
    # feed representative calibration data through the model
    for batch in calib_dataloader:
        model(**batch)

model = mtq.quantize(model, mtq.INT8_DEFAULT_CFG, forward_loop)

Three things to notice. First, quantization never touches your training code — the only new artifact is forward_loop, a plain callable that runs calibration batches. Second, the config is data: mtq.INT8_DEFAULT_CFG is a dictionary loaded from modelopt_recipes/configs/ptq/presets/model/int8.yaml, so you can deepcopy and edit it — the same docstring shows the custom-config pattern, starting from mtq.INT4_AWQ_CFG and appending an entry that disables the *lm_head* quantizer. Third, because quantization is a registered mode, mtq.quantize(model, cfg, loop) is equivalent to applying the mode through the shared state manager, so modelopt_state/save round-trips work for free. For a first experiment, a small model is enough: run the snippet on any transformers causal LM, inspect a layer (it now carries weight_quantizer and input_quantizer attributes), and call the real-quantization conversion to see packed weights.

FP8 and NVFP4: Low-Precision Paths

INT8 is the baseline, but the interesting files in this repository are the floating-point formats. Presets like FP8_DEFAULT_CFG, L1706 and NVFP4_DEFAULT_CFG, L1740 configure the same quantizer machinery for E4M3 and 4-bit floating point with two-level block scales. On the tensor side, real quantization produces packed objects deriving from BaseQuantizedTensor, L40: FP8QTensor, L33 for per-tensor FP8, and NVFP4QTensor, L67 for NVFP4, where weights are grouped into blocks of sixteen with a per-block E4M3 scale and a per-tensor FP8 scale above it. Sibling files cover MXFP8, MXFP4, INT4, and NF4 — one module per format, one dequantize contract each.

The preset YAMLs under modelopt_recipes/configs/ptq/presets/model/ are worth reading even if you never quantize: nvfp4.yaml shows exactly which module classes get weight-only versus weight-and-activation treatment, and the recipe directory also carries IQ1/IQ2-style entries for extreme weight-only compression. QAT enters through the same facade — quantized replicas are already gradient-carrying, so mts-style mode application plus an optimizer loop is all a training harness needs; NVIDIA’s QAT blog series from 2025 describes this workflow in detail for gpt-oss-class models.

One export detail deserves mention for serving: attention itself needs special handling at FP8, which is why export_onnx.py contains export_fp8_mha, L356 alongside the generic export_int8, L132 and export_fp8, L253 — fused multi-head attention has to survive graph surgery as a unit rather than being decomposed into Q/DQ pairs.

Sparsity, Pruning, and Export

The compression family beyond quantization follows the same shape. Weight sparsity exposes mts.sparsify, which drives searchers such as SparseGPTSearcher, L144 — a one-shot, Hessian-based mask search that zeroes weights and reconstructs the remaining ones to minimize output error — and MagnitudeSearcher for the simpler magnitude criterion. Attention sparsity is a different beast entirely: SparseAttentionModule, L27 replaces dense attention with token-selection logic, and the plugin in plugins/vllm.py implements ModelOptSparseAttentionBackend, L801, a drop-in flash-attention backend so a sparsified model can actually run on the vLLM server rather than merely export to it.

Pruning is search again: mtp.prune, L31 evaluates width and depth candidates, with FastNASModeDescriptor, L327 providing the channel-search mode and a binary searcher that halves or keeps blocks. The practical recipe, demonstrated in NVIDIA’s Minitron work, is prune → distill → quantize — one mode call per stage.

The export layer is where checkpoints meet serving engines. export_hf_checkpoint, L1871 writes a Hugging Face-compatible quantized checkpoint that vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM load natively; capture_quantized_weight_export_state, L375 snapshots the packed weights and scales during that process, and ExportContext, L44 dispatches per-model handlers. For deployment to classic TensorRT engines there is the ONNX path: the model-free quantizer at quantize, L122 inserts Q/DQ into an existing graph, its FP8 sibling at quantize, L140 can upgrade an INT8 graph in place via int8_to_fp8, L56, and the graph-surgery CLI at main, L64 handles the finicky edits (DQ-transpose folding, GQA replacement) that raw ONNX tooling makes painful. If your serving stack is ONNX-centric, our ONNX overview pairs well with this section.

Detail: the quantization core (config, mode, registry, fake-quant kernels) feeds both the real-quantization qtensor formats and the ONNX writers; sparsity searchers and the pruning mode converge on the same unified export that emits quantized checkpoints and TRT-LLM configs.

Honest Limits

The source is honest about what it cannot do, and so should we be. First, layout drift is real: older write-ups (including some NVIDIA docs) reference a modelopt/quantization/ package of standalone low-precision kernels, plus modelopt/core/ and modelopt/experimental/ directories — none of those exist on the current main; the low-precision tensor implementations now live under modelopt/torch/quantization/qtensor/, and preset configs moved into the separate modelopt_recipes package. Second, naming drift: mtq.int8-style preset attributes from 2024 tutorials are gone; the constants are INT8_DEFAULT_CFG and friends. Third, hardware: FP8 kernels target Hopper and newer, NVFP4 targets Blackwell; on unsupported GPUs the fake-quant simulation runs, but you are measuring accuracy potential, not speed. Fourth, accuracy is never guaranteed — INT8 SmoothQuant is usually free, W4A16 AWQ is usually close, but W4A4 NVFP4 and 2:4 sparsity are trade-offs where QAT or quantization-aware distillation is effectively mandatory. Finally, the library is pre-1.0 with a one-release deprecation window, so pin your version. Few compression toolkits make their entire surface — calibrators, fake-quant autograd, sparse attention kernels, graph surgery — this readable.
entry.summary: Walk through the ModelOpt source: INT8/FP8 PTQ and QAT flows, weight sparsity, pruning, and export paths into TensorRT and vLLM.

entry.title: TensorRT Source Tour: From ONNX Graph to Serialized CUDA Engine

link.title: TensorRT Source Tour: From ONNX Graph to Serialized CUDA Engine

entry.content:
Most deep-learning frameworks you meet day to day are executors: they take a graph, schedule its ops, and hope the kernels underneath are fast. TensorRT is a different animal. It is a compiler: it ingests a trained network, picks concrete CUDA kernels for every layer by timing candidates on your actual GPU, fuses what it can, and emits a self-contained, version-locked binary called an engine. The OSS repository we are touring today — NVIDIA/TensorRT, currently at version 11.4 — contains the public C++ API headers, the reference plugin library, the ONNX ingest layer, and the build scaffolding; the closed-source libnvinfer binary does the heavy lifting underneath them. Reading these headers is the best way to understand what the compiler promises you, which is exactly what this post walks through.

If you have followed our earlier tours of ONNX as the interchange format and of TensorRT-LLM as the LLM-focused sibling project, this is the foundation those posts stood on. TensorRT consumes ONNX as its primary input — the parser that converts a protobuf graph into TensorRT’s own INetworkDefinition lives right in this repository (well, its header does; the implementation is the onnx-tensorrt submodule). Everything else — tactic selection, plugin resolution, serialization — flows from the two dozen interfaces declared in include/.

The codebase is organized around a clean split. The build side (include/NvInfer.h) owns network construction and engine compilation; the runtime side (include/NvInferRuntime.h) owns deserialization and execution; the plugin side (include/NvInferPluginBase.h, include/NvInferRuntimeCommon.h, and the entire plugin/ tree) lets you extend the compiler with custom layers. Every public handle forwards to an opaque mImpl pointer, so the ABI can evolve without breaking recompiles — you will see the same VImpl pattern in ONNX Runtime and other ABI-sensitive projects.

TensorRT end to end: the ONNX parser fills an INetworkDefinition, the builder compiles it into a serialized engine plan, the runtime deserializes it into an ICudaEngine, and the plugin ecosystem extends the compiler with custom ops registered into a global registry.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • IParser, L191 — the ONNX front-end interface: parse(), parseFromFile(), and error reporting are the whole contract.
  • createParser, L755 — the factory that binds a parser to a network definition and a logger; from here on the parser writes layers directly into your network.
  • INetworkDefinition, L8168 — the framework-neutral graph TensorRT actually optimizes: tensors, layers, and marked outputs.
  • buildSerializedNetwork, L11739 — the compiler entry point on IBuilder: it times tactics, builds profiles, and returns a serialized engine plan as IHostMemory.
  • IRuntime, L1900 — the runtime-side factory; deserializeCudaEngine turns the plan back into a live engine.
  • deserializeCudaEngine, L2032 — where the serialized blob becomes an executable object again, plugins resolved from the registry.
  • ICudaEngine, L3143 — the immutable, per-GPU compiled artifact; it can spawn any number of execution contexts.
  • IExecutionContext, L4089 — the mutable per-stream state: set input shapes, bind device addresses, call enqueueV3.
  • IPluginRegistry, L55 — the global creator table both the builder and the runtime consult when a layer name has no built-in implementation.

The Build Side: Network, Builder, Config

Everything starts with two factory calls. createInferBuilder (NvInfer.h, L11916) gives you an IBuilder, and createNetworkV2 (NvInfer.h, L11662) mints an empty INetworkDefinition. In TensorRT 11 the explicit-batch flag that dominated 10.x documentation is gone — dynamic shapes are simply how the network works, described through optimization profiles rather than a creation flag.

Programmatically constructing a network is pleasingly mechanical: every layer type — convolutions, matmuls, elementwise ops, shuffles — is one method on INetworkDefinition, each returning a typed layer handle whose inputs and outputs are ITensor objects. You wire tensors together, then call markOutput (NvInfer.h, L8222) on whatever tensors escape the network. In practice almost nobody hand-builds graphs anymore; the ONNX parser does it, and (as the diagram shows) the parser is just another producer of the same graph IR.

The interesting object is IBuilderConfig (NvInfer.h, L10622). This is where precision flags (setFlag at NvInfer.h, L10725 for FP16, INT8, FP8, sparsity), workspace budgets via setMemoryPoolLimit (NvInfer.h, L11081), profiles, and DLA targeting all live. One builder can serve many configs; one config fully determines how aggressive the compiler gets. Memory is a first-class concern — the pool limits bound tactic workspace, persistent cache, and weight-streaming pools separately, which matters enormously once you target embedded GPUs where every megabyte is contested.

The detail view: how the ONNX ingest chain, the build/tactics surface, the runtime execution trio, and the plugin ecosystem connect — one node per source file, every node linked to the real code.

Tactics and the Timing Cache

“Tactic” is TensorRT’s word for a concrete kernel-scheduling choice for one layer: which convolution algorithm, which fusion grouping, which memory layout. At build time the compiler enumerates plausible tactics per layer and times each one on your GPU, keeping the winner. The knobs you control are TacticSource bits (NvInferRuntime.h, L2885) — in 11.x just kEDGE_MASK_CONVOLUTIONS and kJIT_CONVOLUTIONS remain, toggled through setTacticSources (NvInfer.h, L10981). The header comment on the JIT source is refreshingly honest: enabling it “may increase” engine building time.

Because re-timing hundreds of tactics on every build is painful, TensorRT persists the measurements. createTimingCache (NvInfer.h, L11016) returns an ITimingCache (NvInfer.h, L10209) that you attach to the config; after a build, ITimingCache::serialize (NvInfer.h, L10223) hands you a blob you can check in next to your model. CI farms love this: build once per driver/GPU family, replay the cache everywhere. The catch is documented right in the header — a cache “must be generated by a build of exact same version,” so caches, like engines, are version-locked artifacts rather than durable data.

The end product of all this measurement is not a live object but bytes: buildSerializedNetwork (NvInfer.h, L11739) returns IHostMemory containing the plan. Engines are only consumable by the same TensorRT version on the same compute capability — a deliberate trade: the compiler freezes GPU-specific decisions in exchange for not shipping a kernel-selection runtime. Serialization is also how the ecosystem moves engines around; serving stacks like Triton Inference Server treat the plan file as the deployable unit, exactly the role an .onnx file plays for ONNX Runtime.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s fast path is one command: pip install tensorrt — the Python package wraps the same C++ API, so the concepts below transfer one-to-one. For the full OSS build you need CUDA 12.9 or 13.4, CMake ≥ 3.31, then git clone -b main https://github.com/nvidia/TensorRT TensorRT && git submodule update --init --recursive, and the release tarballs from NVIDIA provide libnvinfer plus the trtexec CLI you can use to sanity-check engines without writing code.

Here is the whole build-to-execute flow in C++, using only interfaces we verified in the tree above:

#include "NvInfer.h"
#include "NvOnnxParser.h"

using namespace nvinfer1;

Logger logger;  // your ILogger implementation

// Build side: compile model.onnx into a serialized engine plan.
auto builder = std::unique_ptr<IBuilder>(createInferBuilder(logger));
auto network = std::unique_ptr<INetworkDefinition>(builder->createNetworkV2(0));
auto parser  = std::unique_ptr<IParser>(nvonnxparser::createParser(*network, logger));
parser->parseFromFile("model.onnx", static_cast<int>(ILogger::Severity::kWARNING));

auto config = std::unique_ptr<IBuilderConfig>(builder->createBuilderConfig());
auto plan   = std::unique_ptr<IHostMemory>(
    builder->buildSerializedNetwork(*network, *config));

// Runtime side: deserialize and execute on a CUDA stream.
auto runtime = std::unique_ptr<IRuntime>(createInferRuntime(logger));
auto engine  = std::unique_ptr<ICudaEngine>(
    runtime->deserializeCudaEngine(plan->data(), plan->size()));
auto context = std::unique_ptr<IExecutionContext>(engine->createExecutionContext());
// set tensor addresses, then: context->enqueueV3(stream);

Every symbol in that snippet is real: createInferBuilder (NvInfer.h, L11916), createNetworkV2 (NvInfer.h, L11662), createBuilderConfig (NvInfer.h, L11635), parseFromFile (NvOnnxParser.h, L222), and on the runtime side createInferRuntime (NvInferRuntime.h, L5226), deserializeCudaEngine (NvInferRuntime.h, L2032), and createExecutionContext (NvInferRuntime.h, L3301). Actual GPU work is submitted asynchronously by enqueueV3 (NvInferRuntime.h, L4791) on a stream you own — there is no blocking execute dance anymore, and multi-stream serving is just more contexts on more streams.

The Plugin Registry and IPluginV3

When the parser meets an ONNX op TensorRT does not implement, or when you have a hand-written CUDA kernel no graph rewrite can express, plugins are the escape hatch. The current contract is IPluginV3 (NvInferPluginBase.h, L205), a versioned interface whose key move is the capability split: a plugin object returns separate interfaces for the kCORE, kBUILD, and kRUNTIME phases. Build-phase code answers “what output shapes and formats can you support”; runtime-phase code does the actual launch. The cleanest example in the tree is ROIAlignV3 (roiAlignPlugin.h, L58), which inherits IPluginV3, IPluginV3OneCore, IPluginV3OneBuild, and IPluginV3OneRuntime on one class.

Registration is a two-lane system. Lane one: REGISTER_TENSORRT_PLUGIN(Creator) (NvInferRuntime.h, L5271) is a static-initializer macro that self-registers a creator when the plugin library loads — see it live at skipLayerNormPlugin.cpp, L41 for the fused Skip-LayerNorm V3 plugin (skipLayerNormPlugin.h, L46). Lane two: the monolithic bundled library calls initLibNvInferPlugins (inferPlugin.cpp, L171), which pushes dozens of creators — ROIAlign, EfficientNMS, InstanceNormalization, GroupNorm — into the PluginCreatorRegistry (inferPlugin.cpp, L152) through registerCreator (NvInferRuntimeCommon.h, L158). Both lanes end in the same registry the builder consults mid-compile.

The tree also documents history. GroupNormalizationPlugin (groupNormalizationPlugin.h, L37) still implements the older IPluginV2DynamicExt shape, with the familiar configurePlugin / enqueue rhythm and the actual CUDA launch at groupNormalizationPlugin.cpp, L127. If you write a new plugin today, target V3 — the V2 surface is kept for compatibility and is not recommended for new work. Note that most of these plugin kernels are plain CUDA in this repo (dive into plugin/common/kernels/ for the shared math); they are an underrated tutorial on writing production tensor kernels, complementary to the template-library style of CUTLASS.

Runtime: Engines, Contexts, and Streams

The runtime side is deliberately tiny. createInferRuntime hands you an IRuntime; its one big method is deserializeCudaEngine. An ICudaEngine is immutable — you can even re-serialize it with serialize (NvInferRuntime.h, L3201) or query which tactic sources actually made it into the compiled plan via getTacticSources (NvInferRuntime.h, L3651). All mutable state lives in IExecutionContext: input shape binding, address binding, and stream-ordered launch. One engine, many contexts, is the canonical serving pattern — each worker thread gets its own context over the shared weights.

Two runtime details deserve a nod. First, hardware targeting: IRuntime::setDLACore (NvInferRuntime.h, L1919) and the builder’s getNbDLACores (NvInfer.h, L11603) expose NVIDIA’s on-SoC deep-learning accelerator as just another backend the same engine format covers. Second, plugin lifetimes at runtime: the deserializer resolves plugin creators through getPluginRegistry (NvInferRuntime.h, L5207), so any engine containing custom ops needs those plugins loaded before deserialization — a classic deployment footgun that the registry design makes visible rather than silent.

Honest Limits

The trade-offs are real and worth naming before you adopt TensorRT for a project:

  • The open source is not the whole compiler. This repository ships headers, the plugin library, and the parser. The tactic-search heuristics, the fusers, and the kernel library itself live in the closed libnvinfer binary. You can read the contract but not the optimizer — the inverse of projects like OpenVINO or ONNX Runtime, where the graph transformations are all in-tree.
  • Build latency is the price of throughput. Tactic timing plus JIT convolution sources can turn an engine build into minutes-long, GPU-pegged work. Timing caches help, but a cache is only valid for the exact TensorRT version (the header says so verbatim), and every version upgrade re-opens the search.
  • Engines are version-locked and hardware-specific. A plan built on one GPU generation will not deserialize on another, and forward compatibility across TensorRT releases is not a design goal. That makes engine artifacts closer to compiled binaries than to portable models — plan your artifact storage accordingly.
  • NVIDIA-only, full stop. No AMD, no Apple, no CPU fallback path. If your deployment matrix is heterogeneous, you will maintain a second serving chain for non-CUDA targets.
  • ONNX coverage has holes. Unsupported ops throw you into plugin territory, which means writing and maintaining CUDA for exactly the layers that made you reach for TensorRT in the first place.

None of these caveats change the punchline: for fixed models on NVIDIA GPUs, the compiler’s willingness to measure before committing is why TensorRT-compiled engines routinely beat interpreted execution by healthy margins. The source tour above should give you the map to go from “it’s fast” to knowing precisely which interface is responsible for the speed — and where to look when something is not.
